newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE-Brazil's poor march for land and justice.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Brazil's poor march for land and justice.

text.p: An army of Brazil's poor is on the march, trudging 750 miles (1,200 km) to demand land to farm and justice for the killers of their dead colleagues.

Carrying rusty farm tools and revolutionary-looking red flags, about 1,000 landless and small-plot farmers, their ranks swelled by unemployed factory workers and beggars, are converging on remote Brasilia in three marches. They plan to set up their communal tents in the heart of the capital on Thursday (April 17), a year to the day since police in a remote corner of the Amazon gunned down 19 peasants also demanding land. No arrests were made in that incident.

"We want to get to Brasilia and go home to some land. That's what we're fighting for and what our friends died for," unemployed electrician Elias Fiel dos Santos said as he rested from his daily 13-mile (20-km) walk on the hot highway.

Like tens of thousands of Brazilians, dos Santos lives in a squalid encampment, hoping the government will soon include him in its program to give land to the landless. As a member of the radical Landless Movement (MST), the self-proclaimed champion of Brazil's underclass, he is also involved in one of the biggest challenges so far to Fernando Henrique Cardoso's 2-year-old presidency.
LANDLESS MOVEMENT EMERGES AS OPPOSITION FORCE

"The left-wing political parties and the trade unions have seized on the MST as a powerful opposition force and the government is perplexed," Brasilia University politics professor David Fleischer said.

The MST was born in 1985 from a Catholic Church group in Brazil's southernmost state, Rio Grande do Sul, a hotbed of leftwing activism since early this century when German and Italian immigrants arrived brimming with the ideas of Marx. With Brazil deep in recession and modern farming techniques throwing thousands out of work, the MST quickly developed into a tightly organized network that transformed illiterate laborers into a disciplined force.

The movement's trademark invasions of unused farmland by thousands of families are carried out with military-style precision, and often at a bloody cost. More than 100 people have died in rural violence since Cardoso took office in 1995.

"We are not an armed group because society would not tolerate that, but the death toll shows there is a class struggle going in Brazil," march organizer Gilberto Barden said as he nursed a pair of painfully swollen ankles.
With public opinion increasingly on its side, the MST says it will quicken the pace of its invasions this year if the government does not speed up its land reform program.

"We're carrying out the widest agrarian reform program in Brazil's history but it's not enough," conceded Agrarian Reform Minister Raul Jungmann, whose job is to meet Cardoso's campaign pledge of settling 280,000 families in four years.
Officials figures show about half of Brazil's farmland belongs to just two percent of landowners, one of the world's worst land distribution ratios.
GOVERNMENT MOVES ON LAND "NOT ENOUGH"

The creation of Jungmann's post was part of the government's response to last year's massacre. It also raised taxes on unused land, introduced new laws to speed up land reform and offered more credit to recently installed settlers.
But the MST dismisses the changes as "tinkering" and says real change is being thwarted by a landowners' lobby in Congress whose support is key to Cardoso's fragile alliance.

"Land reform is not just about handing out land," MST director Gilberto Portes said. "We need to stop cheap grain imports coming in, we must invest in the countryside. That means changing the country's economy and its politics."

There appears little chance of a U-turn like that. The Real Plan economic program introduced by Cardoso as finance minister in 1994 has tamed Brazil's once rampant inflation and given him unprecedented popularity. All the pundits say he will cruise to re-election next year.
MST RIDING HIGH IN PUBLIC OPINION

But his effort to ease Brazil's acute poverty has fallen short of expectations, creating a vacuum filled by the MST. A recent poll found 85 percent of Brazilians supported non-violent land invasions, and a prime-time soap opera that told the love story of a rich farmer and a beautiful landless peasant brought the land issue to millions of living rooms each night.

Faced with its ever-higher profile, Cardoso has softened his tone towards the MST. In late March, with the marchers already headed for Brasilia, he offered the movement the possibility of talks for the first time since last August. A few days later, a high court suspended an arrest warrant for fugitive MST leader Jose Rainha, wanted on murder charges.
But Cardoso also rules out any sudden acceleration of his land reform policy. "It is hypocritical to ask for more, knowing full well there is no money," the president said.
That message is unlikely to satisfy the marchers. After trekking for two months, many pledged they would not leave Brasilia empty-handed.
"Suffering is part of our struggle," Atilio dos Santos said as he fed his 2-year-old daughter Elizete. "As long as we're left without land, we'll be fighting."
